Coupling Interval Variability of Outflow Tract Premature Ventricular Contractions: A Poincaré Plot‐Based Assessment
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Purpose
                    Coupling interval variability (ΔCI) of premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) may provide insight into their site of origin. This study evaluated whether ΔCI, quantified by Poincaré graph analysis, can distinguish PVCs arising from the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) compared to other locations.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We screened 117 patients undergoing electroanatomical mapping and catheter ablation for PVCs. Exclusion criteria included: failed ablation, low PVC burden on Holter ECG, non‐sinus baseline rhythm, or absence of a qualifying Holter recording. Sixty patients met these criteria: 34 with RVOT PVCs, 11 with left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) PVCs, and 15 with non‐RVOT PVCs. ΔCI was assessed using Poincaré plots derived from the Holter ECG recordings.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      A ΔCI < 100 ms predicted RVOT origin with a specificity of 100% and a sensitivity of 25%. Poincaré plots effectively visualized CI variability, with narrow PVC clusters (measured along the
                      x
                      ‐axis) corresponding to RVOT origin. Broader clusters were observed in LVOT and other non‐RVOT PVCs, reflecting greater variability.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    ΔCI, represented by Poincaré plots, is a reliable and time‐efficient marker of RVOT PVC origin. Narrow PVC clusters with low ΔCI strongly suggest RVOT localization, offering a practical adjunct to vectographic mapping in clinical ablation strategies.

title: Cerebral Safety of Two Pulsed Field Ablation Workflows for Pulmonary Vein Isolation: Results From the Randomized TWOSOME MRI Study
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Data on silent cerebral events/lesions (SCE/SCL) following pulsed field ablation (PFA) for pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) are limited. This study aimed to assess the incidence of SCE/SCL using cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI) in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients undergoing PVI with two distinct PFA systems and workflows.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    In this prospective, single‐center TWOSOME MRI substudy, patients with paroxysmal AF were randomized 1:1 to single‐shot or single‐tip PFA. Single‐shot PVI was performed using a pentaspline PFA catheter (single‐transseptal access, PV‐angiography, no 3D mapping) and single‐tip PVI using a PFA generator with a focal ablation catheter (double‐transseptal access, 3D mapping). A predefined consecutive cohort underwent 1.5‐T cMRI 24 h after the procedure. SCE were defined as acute cMRI‐detected lesions resolving on 6‐week follow‐up cMRI, and SCL as persistent lesions. Baseline characteristics, neurological symptoms, procedural data, and cMRI findings were assessed.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Fifty patients underwent cMRI (25 per group). Acute SCE were detected in 3/50 patients (6%; 95% CI 1.3–16.5), with 1/25 (4%) in the single‐shot group and 2/25 (8%) in the single‐tip group (
                      p
                       = 1.00). All SCE resolved on follow‐up imaging, with no evidence of persistent SCL. One symptomatic stroke occurred in the single‐shot group, unrelated to PFA, and was attributed to air embolization during transseptal puncture. No permanent neurological deficits occurred.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    
                      In this exploratory cMRI study, both PFA workflows showed a low incidence of SCE without evidence of SCL or PFA‐related neurological complications. Larger studies are required to compare cerebral safety profiles of PFA technologies.

title: Preprocedural Computed Tomography Guidance Improves Accuracy of Right Ventricular Septal Lead Placement in Pacemaker Implantation
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Accurate right ventricular septal lead placement is crucial for optimal pacemaker performance and procedural safety, yet conventional fluoroscopy‐guided implantation is limited by inter‐individual anatomical variability. We therefore examined whether preprocedural computed tomography (CT) can provide patient‐specific anatomical guidance to enable precise lead positioning.
                  
                  
                    Methods and Results
                    
                      We retrospectively analyzed 501 consecutive patients who underwent initial dual‐chamber pacemaker implantation for bradycardia pacing (non‐CT‐guided,
                      n
                       = 243; CT‐guided,
                      n
                       = 258). In the CT‐guided group, the midseptal target was determined preoperatively using multiplanar reconstruction of CT images, and reference lines were projected onto the scout image to guide lead placement. We evaluated the total procedure time, fluoroscopy time, right ventricular lead electrical parameters, implantation site, and complications. CT guidance was associated with a higher rate of septal lead placement than non‐CT guidance (93.0% vs. 55.6%,
                      p
                       < 0.001), whereas free‐wall lead placement was less frequent (7.0% vs. 44.4%,
                      p
                       < 0.001). The procedural radiation dose was lower with CT guidance (CT‐guided, 100.2 ± 124.6 mGy vs. non‐CT‐guided, 169.1 ± 152.4 mGy;
                      p
                       < 0.001). Among patients with complete atrioventricular block and available postoperative paced QRS measurements (
                      n
                       = 303), QRS duration was shorter in the CT‐guided group than in the non‐CT‐guided group (145.3 ± 22.3 ms [
                      n
                       = 165] vs. 155.4 ± 19.0 ms [
                      n
                       = 138],
                      p
                       < 0.001). The association persisted after multivariable adjustment ((adjusted OR, 10.30; 95% CI, 5.91–17.97;
                      p
                       < 0.001). The total procedure time, fluoroscopy time, and pacing parameters were comparable between the groups. Complication rates were low overall, and pocket hematoma was less frequent in the CT‐guided group (0.4% vs. 2.9%,
                      p
                       = 0.03).
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    Preprocedural CT guidance facilitated precise planning of the right ventricular lead target using scout images and was associated with accurate and reproducible placement at the intended septal site without prolonging procedural time or compromising electrical performance. This approach may represent a practical strategy for optimizing lead placement in bradycardia pacing.

title: Cavotricuspid Isthmus Ablation Using a Variable Loop Pulsed Field Ablation Catheter: A Single‐Center Descriptive Analysis
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation is frequently performed concomitant with pulmonary vein isolation (PVI). Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as the preferred energy source for PVI, but it is unclear whether CTI ablation can be performed with PFA catheters.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We retrospectively analyzed data from patients who underwent PVI and CTI ablation using a variable‐loop PFA catheter for feasibility, efficacy, and safety.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Twenty‐three patients (mean age 65 years, 57% male) were included in this analysis. Systemic intravenous nitroglycerin was administered to all subjects to prevent vasospasm. Acute CTI block could be documented in all patients at the end of the ablation procedure without complications and with low fluoroscopy exposure. We observed one symptomatic recurrence of possible typical atrial flutter during a mean follow‐up of 218 days.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    CTI ablation using a variable‐loop PFA ablation catheter was feasible, efficient, and safe in the acute setting. Prospective studies with larger patient numbers are needed to evaluate the long‐term efficacy and safety of this approach.

title: Artifactual Contact Force Rise During High‐Power Radiofrequency Delivery With the QDOT MICRO Catheter: A Comparative Study Using Non‐Contact Tests
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Contact force (CF)‐sensing technology ensures effective lesion formation and safety during radiofrequency (RF) ablation; however, the potential for an artifactual rise in CF, a false elevation not attributed to physical contact, remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate and compare the occurrence and magnitude of artifactual CF rise between the QDOT MICRO catheter (QMc) and the Thermocool SmartTouch SF catheter (STSFc) using a non‐contact RF delivery (NCRD) test.
                  
                  
                    Methods and Results
                    
                      We retrospectively analyzed 135 patients who underwent NCRD testing in the right atrium (QMc,
                      n
                       = 93; STSFc,
                      n
                       = 42). The NCRD test was performed in a blood pool without tissue contact at power settings of 90, 50, and 40 W for QMc and 50 and 40 W for STSFc. The magnitude and incidence of CF rise (≥ 5 and ≥ 10 g) were compared.
                    
                    
                      In the QMc group, a significant power‐dependent increase in CF was observed: 9 g (IQR: 5–12 g) at 90 W, 3 g (IQR: 1–10 g) at 50 W, and 2 g (IQR: 1–3 g) at 40 W (
                      p
                       < 0.001). At 90 W, the incidence of CF rise ≥ 5 g was 76%, and that of CF rise ≥ 10 g was 46%, significantly higher than at lower settings. In contrast, the STSFc group exhibited stable CF measurements with no instances of CF rise ≥ 5 g. QMc also showed significant power‐dependent elevation in electrode temperature.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    QMc exhibited significant power‐dependent artifactual CF rise. These findings suggest that catheter‐specific design and thermal effects may influence CF stability during RF delivery. Preprocedural NCRD tests may help identify catheter‐specific CF instability before CF‐guided ablation.

Frequent Premature Ventricular Complexes and Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background and Aims
                    Frequent premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) are often observed in patients undergoing ablation of atrial fibrillation (AF). However, the relationship between AF ablation and PVCs is uncertain. The purpose of this study was to examine the prevalence of frequent PVCs before and after catheter ablation of AF.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    This was a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing ablation of AF at two tertiary centers. All patients undergoing initial or repeat ablation of AF were eligible. Patients were followed in AF clinics before and after ablation with routine ambulatory ECG monitoring.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    The cohort consisted of 421 patients (mean 63 years, 33% female, 57% paroxysmal). At baseline, 18.4% and 4.7% had ≥ 1% and ≥ 5% PVCs respectively. In the 179 days post‐ablation, 9.0% developed new onset ≥ 1% PVCs, whereas 10.9% of patients had regression from ≥ 1% to < 1% PVCs. In the total follow up period of 2 years, there was a significant increase in the proportion of patients with ≥ 1% PVCs. Multivariable modeling revealed baseline PVC burden and hypertension as the only predictors of an increasing PVC burden in the post‐ablation period.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    Frequent PVCs are highly prevalent among patients undergoing AF ablation. However, there was no signal of an increase in frequent PVCs in the immediate post‐ablation period.

Cellular consequences of non-ablative radiotherapy, a novel approach to ventricular tachycardias
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background and aims
                    Radiotherapy (RT) with a single application of ionizing radiation (STAR) has been suggested as a non-invasive alternative to radiofrequency in ablating ventricular tachycardia (VT). Emerging data reveal that STAR may suppress VT without substrate destruction, by enhancing impulse conduction instead, through increased expression of NaV1.5 channels and connexin 43. The study aims to investigate electrophysiology and intracellular Ca2+ dynamics in cardiomyocytes (CMs) from mice subjected to in-vivo RT. The emerging data led us to evaluate biochemical changes potentially linking electrophysiological response to ionizing irradiation.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    CMs isolated 2 weeks after RT with low-dose (15 Gy) or high-dose (25 Gy) were compared to those of sham-treated mice (CTRL). We evaluated: i) the properties of the transient (INaT) and sustained (INasus) components of INa; ii) AP parameters, including the prevalence of Early After-Depolarizations (EADs); iii) intracellular Ca2+ dynamics; iv) CaMKII phosphorylation and v) ROS content.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    25 Gy RT i) increased INaT and, to a larger extent, INasus (increased INasus/INaT ratio); ii) increased AP amplitude, +dV/dtMAX and duration (APD) and facilitated EADs; iii) depressed intracellular Ca2+ dynamics. 15 Gy RT had similar but smaller effects (dose-dependency). 25 Gy RT reduced CaMKII phosphorylation but increased cell ROS content, thus providing a mechanism for the late component of INa (INaL) enhancement.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    The results support the view that STAR may supress VT by increasing conduction velocity, with APD prolongation providing an additional mechanism. On the other hand, INasus enhancement and Ca2+ handling depression may impair electrical stability and contractility in the irradiated region.

title: Coexistance of Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity and Orthostatic Hypotension in Patients with Unexplained Syncope
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background
                    Carotid sinus hypersensitivity (CSH) and orthostatic hypotension (OH) are established causes of syncope but are often considered separate entities. However, evidence suggests that CSH and OH may coexist and jointly contribute to syncope. This study investigates the relationship between CSH and OH in patients with unexplained syncope.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A total of 1,908 patients aged ≥40 years (age, 63.7 ± 13.0 years; men, 45.3%) with unexplained syncope underwent carotid sinus massage (CSM) and head-up tilt testing (HUT). Occurrence of CSH in classical and delayed OH, including asystolic CSM responses was analysed.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Six-hundred-and-eighteen patients (32.4%, 68.9 ± 11.3 years) had OH, while CSH was present in 320 patients (16.8%, 72.2 ± 9.9 years), and was more common in patients with OH than without OH (24.1% vs. 13.3%, p &lt; 0.001). Among patients with CSH, 46.6% also had OH. CSH occurred equally in both classical OH (62/275, 22.5%) and delayed OH (87/345, 25.2%). Among OH patients, CSH was associated with older age, male sex, lower supine diastolic blood pressure, hypertension, and syncope-related hospital admission. An asystolic CSM response was observed more often in OH patients (n = 42; 6.8%) compared with non-OH patients (n = 44, 3.4%, p &lt; 0.001) and was associated with older age and lower resting heart rate.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    CSH and OH frequently coexist in adults over 40 years evaluated for syncope. CSM may reveal a clinically relevant cardioinhibitory reflex in a subgroup of OH patients, supporting comprehensive cardiovascular autonomic testing in unexplained syncope.

title: Safety and Outcomes of Percutaneous Vegetation Aspiration During Transvenous Lead Extraction: A Multicenter Experience
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Transvenous lead extraction (TLE) for cardiac implantable electronic device infection has high procedural success, but with a 1‐year mortality approaching 25%. Potential mechanisms include septic embolization and persistent infected lead casts or “ghosts.” Percutaneous mechanical aspiration of lead‐related vegetations during TLE is a potential strategy to reduce vegetation burden, but safety and outcomes data are limited.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    To describe a multicenter experience utilizing percutaneous vegetation aspiration during TLE, including vegetation characteristics, procedural techniques, complications, and outcomes.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A retrospective multicenter registry included patients undergoing aspiration of lead‐related masses at the time of TLE between 2016 and 2024 across six institutions. Clinical, microbiologic, and procedural data were collected. Vegetation size and outcomes were assessed using transesophageal or intracardiac echocardiography.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Fifty‐three patients (62 ± 14 years, 28% female) underwent aspiration of 63 vegetations during extraction of 114 leads (mean dwell time 9.0 ± 8.2 years). Indications included bacteremia in 44 (83%), fungemia in 4 (8%), fever of unknown origin in 1 (2%), and aseptic thrombus debulking in 4 (8%). Mean vegetation size was 2.8 ± 1.8 cm. Aspiration devices included Penumbra Indigo (34%), Inari FlowTriever (30%), and AngioVac (36%). Complete aspiration occurred in 40 patients (75%). TLE achieved complete success in 49 (92%) and clinical success in 52 (98%). Major complications related to aspiration occurred in 2 patients (4%). After a median follow‐up of 139 days, 10 patients (19%) died.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    Percutaneous vegetation aspiration during TLE appears feasible and generally safe. However, mortality following extraction for device‐related infection remains substantial, and the impact of adjunctive aspiration on outcomes requires further study.

title: Open‐Irrigated Versus Non‐Irrigated Catheters in SVT Ablation: Substrate‐Specific Outcomes in AVRT and AVNRT
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Open‐irrigated catheters (OIC) provide improved cooling, deeper lesion formation, and enhanced safety during radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA). However, comparative evidence regarding substrate‐specific outcomes with OIC versus non‐irrigated catheters (NIC) for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) remains limited. This study compared acute ablation success (AAS) and recurrence after first‐time RFCA using OIC versus NIC, with particular emphasis on differential outcomes in atrioventricular re‐entrant tachycardia (AVRT) and atrioventricular re‐entrant tachycardia (AVNRT).
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A retrospective cohort of consecutive patients undergoing first‐time RFCA for AVNRT or AVRT between 2017 and 2023 was analyzed. Patients were categorized by catheter type (OIC vs. NIC). Primary outcomes were AAS and SVT recurrence during 24‐month follow‐up. Multivariate logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used for adjusted analyses. Subgroup analyses were performed for AVNRT and AVRT.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Among 302 procedures, OIC were used in 113 (37.4%). Overall AAS was achieved in 85.4% of cases (92.0% OIC vs. 81.5% NIC;
                      p
                      = 0.012). Recurrence occurred in 17.9% (7.1% OIC vs. 24.3% NIC;
                      p
                      < 0.001). In multivariable analyses, OIC use was independently associated with higher AAS (adjusted RR 1.12; 95% CI 1.05–1.20;
                      p
                      = 0.001) and lower recurrence (adjusted HR 0.24; 95% CI 0.12–0.52;
                      p
                      < 0.001). In the AVRT subgroup, OIC use was associated with higher AAS (89.9% vs. 76.6%;
                      p
                      = 0.014) and lower recurrence (adjusted HR 0.25; 95% CI 0.11–0.57;
                      p
                      < 0.001), whereas no significant differences were observed in AVNRT.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    In this cohort, OIC use was associated with higher AAS and lower recurrence, with the favorable association primarily observed in AVRT rather than AVNRT. These findings support further evaluation of substrate‐specific catheter selection, particularly for accessory pathway ablation.

title: Pulsed Field Versus Radiofrequency Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation: Esophageal Lesions and Suspected Gastroparesis

                    Background
                    Esophageal mucosal injury and gastroparesis are clinically important complications of radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of atrial fibrillation (AF). Pulsed‐field ablation (PFA) is a non‐thermal modality that may spare these complications due to its myocardial tissue selectivity.

Leadless Pacemakers After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Meta‐analysis With Time‐to‐Event Analysis
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Permanent pacemaker implantation is a common complication after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Leadless pacemakers (LPs) may reduce lead‐ and pocket‐related complications, but their clinical outcomes after TAVR remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta‐analysis evaluated the safety and effectiveness of LPs compared with transvenous pacemakers (TVPs).
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched from inception to June 10, 2026. Randomized and observational studies were included. Random‐effects meta‐analyses pooled proportions, risk ratios (RRs), and mean differences (MDs). Reconstructed Kaplan–Meier data were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs).
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Ten studies involving 10,809 patients (1030 LP and 9779 TVP recipients) were included. The pooled procedural success rate of LP implantation was 98% (95% CI 95%–99%). Implantation success was comparable between LP and TVP (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.98–1.02). Sensitivity analysis demonstrated a shorter hospital stay with LP (MD −1.37 days, 95% CI −2.33 to −0.41) and a lower risk of heart failure hospitalization (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.14–0.96). Overall survival did not differ between groups (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.44–1.23), although reconstructed survival curves showed late separation favoring LP. Device‐related and vascular complications were comparable between LP and TVP.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    LP implantation after TAVR demonstrates excellent procedural success and clinical outcomes comparable to TVPs. LPs may reduce hospital stay and heart failure hospitalization, supporting their use as an alternative pacing strategy in appropriately selected patients.

abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) progression is a recognized complication of cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) implantation, yet its prognostic impact on long‐term clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined.
                  
                  
                    Methods and Results
                    
                      In this single‐center retrospective cohort, 303 patients undergoing CIED implantation between 2005 and 2023 were followed for a median of 4.8 years. TR severity was assessed echocardiographically at baseline and 12 months. The primary endpoint was TR progression (≥ 1‐grade worsening); secondary endpoints were all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, their composite, and progression to severe TR, analyzed by Kaplan–Meier and Cox regression. TR progressed in 103 patients (34.0%), regressed in 33 (10.9%), and remained stable in 167 (55.1%), a net rightward shift (
                      p
                       < 0.001). Progression differed by device type (
                      p
                       = 0.031): among the larger subgroups, VVI‐ICD showed the greatest net progression (31.8% worsened vs. 6.9% improved;
                      p
                       < 0.001) and CRT‐D the highest regression (18.8%). During follow‐up, 67 patients (22.1%) died and 164 (54.1%) were hospitalized. Overall TR progression was not independently associated with mortality (HR 1.118,
                      p
                       = 0.693) but independently predicted cardiovascular hospitalization (HR 1.640,
                      p
                       = 0.003) and the composite endpoint (HR 1.480,
                      p
                       = 0.014). On unadjusted analysis, progression specifically to severe TR (
                      n
                       = 15) was associated with increased mortality (HR 1.99,
                      p
                       = 0.024) and cardiovascular hospitalization (HR 2.45,
                      p
                       < 0.001).
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    TR progression occurs in approximately one‐third of CIED recipients within the first year and independently predicts cardiovascular hospitalization. Progression to severe TR identifies a higher‐risk subset, supporting routine post‐implant echocardiographic surveillance.

title: Association Between Baseline Cognitive Impairment and Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence After Catheter Ablation
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Cognitive impairment is common among patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), yet its prognostic significance in the context of catheter ablation remains unclear.
                  
                  
                    Aims
                    We aimed to investigate whether baseline cognitive impairment, assessed by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), was associated with post‐ablation AF recurrence.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    Based on the China‐AF Registry, we identified 2692 patients with nonvalvular AF who underwent index catheter ablation and had baseline MoCA assessments from 2022 to 2024. Patients were stratified into mild cognitive impairment (MCI, MoCA ≤ 26) and normal cognition (MoCA > 26) groups. The primary outcome was AF recurrence beyond the blanking period. The secondary outcome was a composite of all‐cause death, ischemic stroke, and major bleeding. To adjust for confounding factors, we applied inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) methodology. Weighted Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs).
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      After IPTW adjustment, all baseline covariates were well balanced (all standardized mean differences < 0.03). Over a median follow‐up of 218 days (IQR, 192–376), the MCI group had a significantly higher risk of AF recurrence (aHR 1.48; 95% CI, 1.27–1.73;
                      p
                       <  0.001). The composite secondary endpoint did not demonstrate a statistically significant between‐group difference (aHR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.25–4.52;
                      p
                      = 0.945). The association between baseline MCI and AF recurrence was consistent across all prespecified subgroups (all
                      p
                      for interaction > 0.05).
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    In this large prospective registry study, an independent association was observed between baseline cognitive impairment and an elevated risk of post‐ablation AF recurrence. Cognitive assessment may be useful for risk stratification but requires external validation.

                    Clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT06987825.

title: Timing of Catheter Ablation After Heart Failure Diagnosis for Atrial Fibrillation: A Propensity‐Score‐Matched Analysis
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background
                    Catheter ablation improves outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (HF). However, most of the evidence on the importance of ablation timing has been anchored to AF rather than HF onset, leaving the optimal interval between HF diagnosis and ablation incompletely defined.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    To evaluate the association between the timing of catheter ablation following the first diagnosis of HF and subsequent clinical outcomes in patients with established AF.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We performed a retrospective propensity‐score‐matched cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network. Adults (≥18 years) with AF who subsequently developed HF and underwent catheter ablation were included. The primary analysis compared ablation from day 1 through 3 months after HF diagnosis with ablation at least 91 days after HF diagnosis. Propensity‐score matching yielded 2,570 patients in each group. Outcomes were assessed for 2 years after ablation and included all‐cause mortality, electrical cardioversion, emergency department or inpatient encounters, and HF exacerbation. A 1‐year timing threshold and analyses stratified by recorded left ventricular ejection fraction were examined as sensitivity analyses.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Mean follow‐up was 549.3±253.2 days after early ablation and 534.1±255.3 days after later ablation. Mortality was similar between groups (11.0% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio [HR] 1.078, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.910–1.276;
                      p
                      = 0.384), as were emergency department or inpatient encounters (66.2% vs 65.6%; HR 1.006, 95% CI 0.940–1.076;
                      p
                      = 0.865). Early ablation was associated with fewer cardioversions (15.0% vs 18.6%; HR 0.788, 95% CI 0.689–0.901;
                      p
                      < 0.001) and fewer HF exacerbation events (39.5% vs 46.0%; HR 0.824, 95% CI 0.758–0.896;
                      p
                      < 0.001). The 1‐year timing analysis showed a similar pattern for cardioversion and the HF exacerbation.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    Among patients with AF and HF who ultimately underwent ablation, ablation within 3 months of HF diagnosis was associated with fewer subsequent cardioversions and HF exacerbations than ablation performed from day 91 onward. However, there was no significant difference in mortality between the two cohorts. These findings identify the first months after HF diagnosis as a clinically relevant period for reassessing rhythm‐control strategy and warrant prospective evaluation of ablation timing after HF recognition.

title: Blanking Period after Atrial Fibrillation Catheter Ablation: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Atrial arrhythmias that recur within the first 3 months after atrial fibrillation (AF) catheter ablation are conventionally attributed to a “blanking period” and not classified as procedural failure. Accumulating evidence suggests that such early recurrences of atrial tachyarrhythmias (ERAT) may instead predict late recurrence, raising concern that the conventional 3‐month window overestimates the duration during which recurrences are benign.
                  
                  
                    Objective
                    To assess the association between ERAT during each of the first 3 months after AF catheter ablation and late recurrence of atrial tachyarrhythmias (LRAT), and whether this association differs by ablation energy source.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science without restriction on date or publication status for studies of AF catheter ablation reporting ERAT during defined intervals of the blanking period, stratified by subsequent LRAT status. Ablation energy sources included radiofrequency, cryoballoon, and pulsed field. The exposure was ERAT during the first, second, and third months after ablation, and the outcome was LRAT. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random‐effects models.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Twelve studies comprising 7,751 patients (2,505 with LRAT, 5,246 without) were included. Mean follow‐up was 22.0 months, mean age 60.7 years, 25.8% were women, 52.5% had paroxysmal AF, mean CHA
                      2
                      DS
                      2
                      ‐VASc score was 2.1, mean left atrial diameter 42.6 mm, and mean left ventricular ejection fraction 58.1%. ERAT was associated with subsequent LRAT, and the strength of this association increased across the blanking period: month 1 (12 studies; OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.01–3.08;
                      p
                      = 0.05), month 2 (10 studies; OR 3.46, 95% CI 2.15–5.57;
                      p
                      < 0.001), and month 3 (10 studies; OR 21.4, 95% CI 10.9–42.2;
                      p
                      < 0.001). The graded association was reproduced within the radiofrequency and cryoballoon subgroups.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    ERAT was associated with subsequent LRAT throughout the blanking period, with a graded relationship that strengthened month by month and was strongest in the third month. These findings support a blanking period shorter than the conventional 3 months.

title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure Versus Oral Anticoagulation for Prevention of Stroke or Systemic Embolism in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation: An Updated Meta‐Analysis of 7004 Patients Across Six Randomized Trials
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an emerging alternative for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) who are unsuitable for long‐term oral anticoagulants (OACs). However, its efficacy and safety relative to OACs remain uncertain.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    Three databases were searched up to April 7, 2026, for randomized controlled trials comparing LAAC with OAC in patients with AF. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals were pooled using a random‐effects model.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Six RCTs (
                      n
                       = 7004 patients) were analyzed. The risk of stroke or systemic embolism (SSE) did not differ significantly between the LAAC and OAC groups (RR: 1.10 [0.87–1.39];
                      p
                       = 0.42). The risk of ischemic SSE was significantly increased with LAAC (RR: 1.41 [1.07–1.85];
                      p
                       = 0.02) compared with OAC. No significant differences were observed in all‐cause mortality (RR: 0.94 [0.81–1.09]), cardiovascular mortality (RR: 0.91 [0.69–1.21]), non‐cardiovascular mortality (RR: 0.91 [0.75–1.12]), or hemorrhagic stroke (RR: 0.58 [0.29–1.17]). LAAC was associated with a similar risk of overall major bleeding (RR: 0.92 [0.77–1.09]) and low risk of non‐procedural bleeding (RR: 0.61 [0.52–0.73];
                      p
                       < 0.001) compared with OAC. Upon sensitivity analysis comparing LAAC with DOACs, the findings remained consistent across most clinical outcomes.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    LAAC demonstrates comparable risks of SSE and major bleeding to OACs, but is associated with a higher risk of ischemic SSE and reduced non‐procedural bleeding, supporting its use in selected patients at high risk for long‐term bleeding while emphasizing individualized shared decision‐making.

title: Development and Validation of a Novel Contact Force‐Integrated Pulsed Field Quantization Index for Pulmonary Vein Isolation in a Porcine Model
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    There is no bipolar‐specific quantitative ablation index currently available to guide pulsed field ablation (PFA). We aimed to develop and validate a novel contact force (CF)‐integrated pulsed field quantization index (PFQI) for real‐time lesion depth prediction during bipolar PFA.
                  
                  
                    Methods and Results
                    
                      In total, 27 healthy Yorkshire swine were included in a two‐phase preclinical study. In Phase I, a nonlinear multivariable model was developed to derive a novel PFQI incorporating real‐time CF, pulse train number, delivery voltage, and impedance variation. In Phase II, the PFQI was prospectively validated by comparing predicted with actual lesion depth, followed by PFQI‐guided circumferential pulmonary vein isolation (PVI). Acute procedural success, 30‐day PVI durability, and extracardiac safety were evaluated using serial electroanatomic mapping and blinded histopathological examination. Lesion depth was strongly associated with CF, pulse train number, voltage, and impedance change. The PFQI predicted actual depth with high accuracy (
                      R
                       = 0.94,
                      R
                      2
                       = 0.88; validation
                      R
                      2
                       = 0.82, slope = 1.014). In the validation cohort, 92% of predicted depths fell within ±0.75 mm of measured values. PFQI‐guided PVI achieved 100% (6/6) acute isolation and 100% 30‐day durable electrical isolation, with contiguous transmural fibrosis on histology. No collateral phrenic nerve, esophageal, or pulmonary vein injury occurred, and phrenic capture thresholds remained unchanged.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    The PFQI is the first bipolar‐specific, CF‐integrated quantitative metric for PFA, enabling accurate, real‐time lesion depth prediction. PFQI‐guided PVI achieved consistent, durable, and safe PVI in a porcine model, providing a promising operator‐independent quantitative strategy to optimize clinical bipolar PFA for atrial fibrillation.

title: Procedural Outcomes of Leadless Pacemaker Extraction and Retrieval: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis With Descriptive Synthesis of Post‐Implant Management
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Leadless pacemakers reduce lead‐ and pocket‐related complications, but pooled evidence on the procedural outcomes of their extraction and retrieval remains limited.
                  
                  
                    Methods and Results
                    A systematic review and meta‐analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261397097) evaluated leadless pacemaker extraction or retrieval. The primary analysis pooled independent full‐text studies reporting at least three attempted removals using a random‐effects binomial‐normal generalized linear mixed model. Outcomes were procedural success and major retrieval‐related procedural events. Eight studies contributed 303 removal attempts to the primary success analysis, and six studies contributed 293 subjects or procedures to the safety analysis. Pooled procedural success was 89.1% (95% CI, 85.1% to 92.2%), and major retrieval‐related procedural events occurred in 3.8% (95% CI, 2.1% to 6.7%); between‐study heterogeneity was not detected for either outcome. Sensitivity estimates for major events ranged from 3.3% to 4.1%. Reported dwell time before removal ranged from intraprocedural retrieval to 9 years. A secondary descriptive synthesis of 96 clinical publications and five cohorts with complete denominators characterized post‐implant management without cross‐study pooling.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    Leadless pacemaker removal was successful in approximately nine of 10 attempts, while qualifying major retrieval‐related events occurred in approximately four of 100 safety denominators. The certainty of evidence was very low. Post‐implant management patterns varied across cohorts and could not be pooled.

title: Changes in Lead Parameters of Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices After VT/VF Ablation Using a Dual‐Energy Lattice‐Tip Catheter
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Interactions between cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) and pulsed field ablation (PFA) have been studied mainly in the context of atrial ablation, whereas the effects of ventricular ablation using a dual‐energy lattice‐tip catheter on ventricular leads remain unclear.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    This retrospective study involved 79 patients (mean age 60.9 ± 13.6 years) with an implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator or cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator who underwent ventricular ablation using a lattice‐tip catheter between February 2024 and November 2025. Pacing thresholds were assessed before, immediately after, and 3 months after ablation and standardized to a pulse width of 0.4 ms using the Lapicque–Weiss model. Marked acute threshold elevation was defined as an increase in pacing threshold of ≥ 1.0 V immediately after ablation. The anatomical relationship between ablation sites and ventricular lead locations was assessed based on the American Heart Association 17‐segment model of the left ventricle and classified as corresponding when ablation involved the same or opposing ventricular region as the lead location, adjacent when ablation involved a directly adjacent region, and remote otherwise.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Marked acute pacing‐threshold elevation occurred in 5 of 79 right ventricular (RV) leads (6.3%) and 2 of 22 evaluable left ventricular (LV) leads (9.1%). For RV leads, marked threshold elevation occurred in 4 of 14 patients (28.6%) in the corresponding group, 1 of 19 (5.3%) in the adjacent group, and none of 46 (0%) in the remote group. When threshold change was analyzed as a continuous variable, the acute increase was significantly greater in the corresponding group (+ 0.74 V; 95%CI 0.465–1.018) than in the adjacent (+ 0.31 V; 95%CI 0.076–0.550) and remote (+ 0.007 V; 95%CI − 0.145–0.160) groups. For LV leads, the pacing threshold increased significantly after ablation involving the corresponding segment (+ 0.71 V; 95%CI 0.167–1.245), although the overall association between anatomical relationship and threshold change was not significant. At 3 months, pacing thresholds in the corresponding groups were not significantly different from baseline for either RV or LV leads.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    Marked acute pacing‐threshold elevation was observed in both RV and LV leads after ventricular arrhythmia ablation using a dual‐energy lattice‐tip catheter. However, both RV and LV thresholds were no longer significantly different from baseline at 3 months. These findings suggest the importance of considering the anatomical relationship between ablation sites and CIED leads and of careful peri‐procedural assessment of lead function during ventricular ablation.

title: Electrical Alternans With Alternating Left Ventricular Apical Ballooning Mimicking Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy in a Patient With Extreme QT Prolongation
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    We report unique and rare findings of coupled electrical and mechanical alternans in a patient with extreme QT prolongation.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A 5‐year‐old girl with congenital long QT syndrome type 3 developed alternate left ventricular apical ballooning precipitated by mycoplasma pneumonia and azithromycin exposure.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    During atrial pacing, electrocardiography showed beat‐to‐beat alternation not only in T‐wave morphology but also in QRS configuration, ST segment, and QT interval. These electrical changes were tightly associated with mechanical alternans: beats with markedly prolonged QT intervals showed normal left ventricular (LV) contraction, whereas beats with shorter QT intervals and ST elevation exhibited LV apical ballooning. Treatment with mexiletine shortened the QT interval, abolished both electrical and mechanical alternans, and restored normal LV function.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    Alternate LV apical ballooning mimicking Takosubo cardiomyopathy can be seen in a patient with extreme QT prolongation. These findings probably reflected a functional intraventricular conduction block due to marked spatial heterogeneity of repolarization between the LV base and apex.

title: Pulmonary Artery Approach for Radiofrequency Catheter Ablation of Atrial Tachycardia Originating From Left Atrial Post Wall: A Case Report
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    Due to limitations in ablation energy delivery and myocardial wall thickness, endocardial ablation of atrial tachycardia can sometimes be challenging.
                  
                  
                    Methods and Results
                    In this case, ablation of the left atrial posterior wall shifted the earliest endocardial breakthrough site from the posterior wall to the roof, suggesting a potential epicardial origin near left atrial roof. The atrial arrhythmia was successfully eliminated via a right pulmonary artery approach.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    The right pulmonary artery approach may be an effective strategy for ablating epicardial atrial arrhythmias, particularly those originating from the left atrial posterior roof.

abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) has emerged as a non‐pharmacological alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Following the publication of recent CHAMPION‐AF and CLOSURE‐AF trials, an updated synthesis of evidence is warranted to clarify the long‐term comparative efficacy and safety of LAAO versus OAC in patients with AF.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We conducted a systematic review and meta‐analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing LAAO with OAC in adults with AF. A comprehensive search of major databases was performed from inception to April 2026. The primary efficacy outcomes were major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and stroke. The primary safety outcome was non–procedure‐related bleeding. Random‐effects models were used to calculate pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Six RCTs including 7,004 patients (3,681 LAAO; 3,323 OAC) were analyzed. No statistically significant difference was observed for MACE (7.5% vs 6.9%; RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.79‐1.34) or stroke (3.7% vs 3.2%; RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.80‐1.43). LAAO was associated with a significantly lower risk of non‐procedure‐related bleeding (9.8% vs 16.7%; RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.52‐0.77), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of 6.9% and an approximate number needed to treat of 15 based on crude pooled event rates over the observed trial follow‐up. Trial sequential analysis indicated that the accumulated evidence for MACE and stroke remained inconclusive. Comparator‐type subgroup analyses showed no significant interaction for MACE (
                      p
                      = 0.67) or stroke (
                      p
                      = 0.81) between contemporary predominantly‐DOAC and VKA comparator trials.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    LAAO was associated with lower non‐procedure‐related bleeding, while no statistically significant differences were observed for MACE or stroke. The available efficacy evidence remains inconclusive regarding equivalence or non‐inferiority, and larger trials are needed. These findings support individualized consideration of LAAO when the long‐term bleeding burden of anticoagulation is clinically important.

Value of Left Ventricular Low Voltage Area and Ejection Fraction in Predicting End-Stage Heart Failure Outcomes After Ventricular Tachycardia Ablation in Patients With Non-Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
abstract:
BACKGROUND:
                    Patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM) and ventricular tachycardia are at increased risk for adverse HF outcomes, and abnormal left ventricular (LV) substrate identified by endocardial unipolar and bipolar low-voltage areas (LVAs) may aid in risk stratification. This study assessed the association of LV unipolar and bipolar LVAs with end-stage HF outcomes in patients with NICM undergoing ventricular tachycardia ablation.
                  
                  
                    METHODS:
                    
                      Patients with NICM and LV ejection fraction (EF) <50% undergoing ventricular tachycardia ablation from 2019 to 2023 were included. Endocardial voltage mapping defined confluent (>2 cm
                      2
                      ) unipolar LVAs as <8.27 mV and bipolar LVAs as <1.5 mV during sinus or paced rhythm. End-stage HF outcomes included HF death, LV assist device implantation, or heart transplant. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis assessed associations between unipolar/bipolar LVAs and end-stage HF outcomes.
                    
                  
                  
                    RESULTS:
                    
                      One hundred eleven patients with NICM (mean age, 64.6±9.8 years; 81.1% male; mean LVEF, 33.8±11.7%) were included. During a median follow-up of 28.1 months (interquartile range, 18–46), 28 (25.2%) patients experienced end-stage HF outcomes. Unipolar LVA (hazard ratio, 1.03 per 1% increase [95% CI, 1.01–1.05];
                      P
                      =0.002) and LVEF (hazard ratio, 1.04 per 1% decrease [95% CI, 1.00–1.09];
                      P
                      =0.03) were independently associated with higher end-stage HF risk, while bipolar LVA was not (hazard ratio, 0.98, 1% increase [95% CI, 0.96–1.01];
                      P
                      =0.25). A 3-point risk score based on the Youden index, unipolar LVA ≥70% (2 points), 35% to 70% (1 point), and LVEF ≤25% (1 point), had 82.1% sensitivity and 77.1% specificity for predicting end-stage HF in scores ≥2.
                    
                  
                  
                    CONCLUSIONS:
                    In patients with NICM undergoing ventricular tachycardia ablation, unipolar LVA and LVEF are independent predictors of end-stage HF outcomes. Integrating these predictors yields a prognostic score to identify patients at the highest risk of end-stage HF outcomes.

title: Serial Artificial Intelligence ECG-Derived Atrial Fibrillation Probability and Recurrence Risk After Pulsed Field Ablation
abstract:
BACKGROUND:
                    Pulsed field ablation is now widely used for atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation, but atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence remains common and postablation risk tools are limited. We assessed whether a validated sinus‑rhythm artificial intelligence— enabled ECG AF probability score, and its early postablation change, predicts recurrence after pulsed field ablation.
                  
                  
                    METHODS:
                    We studied consecutive patients undergoing index pulsed field ablation across 3 Mayo Clinic sites (February 2024–March 2025) with ≥1 sinus‑rhythm ECG within 180 days preprocedure. Baseline artificial intelligence—enabled ECG AF score (range 0–1) was the mean across baseline ECGs. Recovery indices (RI30/60/90), defined as mean postprocedure artificial intelligence—enabled ECG score within days 1–30/60/90 minus baseline, predicted post‑blanking recurrence using corresponding 30‑, 60‑, and 90‑day blanking windows. The primary outcome was time to first documented AF/atrial flutter/atrial tachycardia episode >30 seconds, ascertained via clinic ECGs, ambulatory monitoring, and device interrogations. Cox regression adjusted for prespecified clinical and echocardiographic covariates assessed associations; Harrell C‑statistic quantified discrimination.
                  
                  
                    RESULTS:
                    
                      Among 1052 patients (67±10 years; 33% women), median baseline score was 0.35; 320 (30%) recurred over 188 days. Higher baseline score independently predicted recurrence (hazard ratio per 0.1 increase, 1.08 [95% CI, 1.03–1.14]). Scores rose on day 0 after ablation, then declined over subsequent weeks, with persistently higher, less‑improving trajectories among patients who recurred (time×recurrence interaction
                      P
                      <0.001). Day 0 score was not independently associated with recurrence after adjustment. Attenuated early recovery (higher recovery index) was independently associated with recurrence, most robustly for RI-90 (hazard ratio per 0.1 increase, 1.15 [95% CI, 1.07–1.24]), and improved discrimination beyond baseline and covariates (C‑statistic, 0.63–0.67; ΔC=0.04). Findings were consistent in a historical thermal ablation cohort.
                    
                  
                  
                    CONCLUSIONS:
                    Baseline and early postablation dynamics of a sinus‑rhythm artificial intelligence—enabled ECG AF probability score are associated with pulsed field ablation recurrence and may aid multivariable risk stratification; prospective validation is warranted.

title: Evolving Mechanisms on Mortality in Atrial Fibrillation: A 25‐Year National Death‐Certificate Analysis
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Atrial fibrillation (AF) prevalence has risen alongside an aging US population and wider adoption of contemporary therapies, yet population‐level changes in mechanisms of death among people with AF remain incompletely characterized. We used National Death Certificate Trends in AF Mortality data to assess 25‐year trends in AF‐related mortality and the contribution of heart failure (HF), stroke, myocardial infarction (MI), and dementia.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We conducted a retrospective analysis of CDC WONDER records for US decedents aged ≥ 35 years with AF listed as a contributing cause of death from 1999 to 2023, coinciding with the implementation of ICD‐10 coding in the CDC database. We quantified all‐cause and cause‐specific mortality rates per 100 000 and stratified trends by age, sex, and race. The analytic cohort included decedents with AF and at least one of four cardiovascular conditions (stroke, dementia, HF, or MI) listed as a primary or contributing cause of death. Confidence intervals were obtained from CDC WONDER outputs or calculated per CDC guidance.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Among 3 273 015 decedents with AF noted on the death certificate, 461 321 had HF, dementia, stroke, or MI listed as a contributing cause. HF emerged as the leading cause/contributor with a steep rise beginning in approximately 2008. Stroke rates were stable or declining, MI‐related mortality remained low and stable, while dementia, particularly stroke‐free dementia, increased significantly in adults ≥ 85 (outpacing stroke among the oldest White decedents since early 2000s). Non‐White groups exhibited higher stroke and HF mortality trends; women ≥ 85 had higher stroke‐related mortality than men.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    Over 25 years, AF‐associated mortality patterns shifted toward HF and stroke‐free dementia while ischemic stroke and MI declined or stabilized. Findings highlight the need to expand AF care beyond stroke prevention to prioritize HF prevention/management, cognitive health, equitable AF‐care pathways to ensure broad access to therapies, and additional studies of targeted interventions to mitigate disease risks.

Reclassifying Single Lead Sinus Rhythm ECGs for Improved AF Recurrence Detection With Deep Learning
abstract:
BACKGROUND:
                    Atrial fibrillation (AF) remains a common outcome after catheter ablation, with recurrence observed in up to 50% of patients within 5 years. Despite extensive research, challenges remain in optimizing observation and prediction windows for AF recurrence assessment. Therefore, we developed and validated a novel deep learning model that reclassifies sinus rhythm based on past and future AF events using single-lead ECG strips from handheld devices.
                  
                  
                    METHODS:
                    Of the 558 participants, 308 with no documented recurrence during study follow-up contributed Benign Sinus strips, while 250 with documented recurrence contributed sinus rhythm strips recorded within ±3 days of an AF event, defined as Severe Sinus strips. Both clinical feature-based models and a deep learning model were used to classify these ECGs according to their proximity to AF recurrence events. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score.
                  
                  
                    RESULTS:
                    The strip-level pretrained deep learning model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.86, with sensitivity of 0.79, and specificity of 0.76. The complementary participant-level clinical feature-based Random Forest benchmark achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.71, sensitivity of 0.58, and specificity of 0.69. Feature-based analyses identified associations involving heart-rate variability, mean R–R interval, female sex, left atrial volume, and mean P-wave duration.
                  
                  
                    CONCLUSIONS:
                    Our dynamic deep learning model reclassifies 30-second single-lead sinus rhythm ECGs based on AF events within ±3 days, transforming a brief ECG snapshot into a summarized indicator of short-term AF risk.

title: Role of Lifestyle and Risk Factor Modification Clinics in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
abstract:
BACKGROUND:
                    Incidence and recurrence of atrial fibrillation (AF) are associated with several lifestyle risk factors. Lifestyle and risk factor modification (LRFM) clinics could have a role in comprehensively addressing AF from a holistic, patient-centered approach to improve clinical outcomes.
                  
                  
                    METHODS:
                    We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating the role of LRFM clinics compared with usual care in patients with AF. The primary end point was atrial arrhythmia recurrence. Secondary end points were AF and heart failure-related hospitalization, cardiovascular death, stroke or transient ischemic attack, and quality-of-life.
                  
                  
                    RESULTS:
                    
                      Eleven randomized controlled trials with a total of 3364 patients were included (5 randomized controlled trials performed in the context of AF ablation). Mean age was 58 to 73 years, 30% were female, and 18% had persistent AF. Duration of follow-up ranged from 3 to 24 months. LRFM clinics significantly reduced the primary end point of arrhythmia recurrence compared with usual care after catheter ablation (odds ratio, 0.34 [95% CI, 0.23–0.51];
                      P
                      <0.001, I
                      2
                      =0%). LRFM clinics also reduced AF-related hospitalization (odds ratio, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.51–0.98];
                      P
                      =0.04, I
                      2
                      =21%) and improved quality-of-life (mean improvement on Short Form 36 Questionnaire, 8.90 [95% CI, 6.91–10.90];
                      P
                      <0.001). There was no detected difference between LRFM clinics and usual care for heart failure-related hospitalization (
                      P
                      =0.16), cardiovascular deaths (
                      P
                      =0.79), or stroke/transient ischemic attack (
                      P
                      =0.83).
                    
                  
                  
                    CONCLUSIONS:
                    In this meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, LRFM clinics reduced AF recurrence after ablation, reduced AF-related hospitalization, and improved quality of life. This study supports a comprehensive multidisciplinary lifestyle risk modification model of care to improve clinical outcomes in patients with AF.

title: NIMA-Related Kinase-7 Activates Atrial Cardiomyocyte NLRP3 Inflammasome and Associates With Occurrence of Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation
Standardized Spark-Pattern Cut-Mode Electrosurgical Bailout Workflow for Difficult Left Bundle Branch Area Pacing Lead Advancement: Procedural and Follow-Up Outcomes From a 15-Patient Case Series
abstract:
BACKGROUND:
                    Electrosurgical facilitation can aid difficult left bundle branch area pacing lead advancement, but standardized delivery patterns, reassessment logic, and follow-up lead performance remain insufficiently defined.
                  
                  
                    METHODS:
                    We retrospectively analyzed 15 consecutive patients undergoing standardized spark-pattern cut-mode electrosurgical bailout after conventional mechanical left bundle branch area pacing lead advancement failed. The generator was operated in unipolar cut-mode at 20 W; spark-pattern delivery denoted brief sliding contact to the exposed cathode segment followed by immediate mechanical readvancement and ECG/electrogram reassessment. A prestandardization sustain-mode polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation event outside the 15-patient cohort informed the safety workflow.
                  
                  
                    RESULTS:
                    Conventional advancement failed in all included patients. Across 50 target-site advancement attempts, spark-pattern cut-mode assistance was activated at 15 final target sites, requiring 1.5±0.6 cycles per patient. Procedural success of left bundle branch area pacing lead deployment was achieved in 15/15. V1 terminal rightward progression occurred in 14/15, jump in 14/15, and split/discrete components in 12/15. Spark-associated premature ventricular complexes occurred in 15/15 but were isolated and self-limited; no nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, sustained ventricular tachycardia, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation, defibrillation, or hemodynamic instability occurred during the standardized workflow. Mean follow-up was 400±170 days; no clinically documented lead malfunction, dislodgement, microdislodgement, loss requiring revision, septal perforation, ventricular septal defect, pericardial effusion, or reintervention occurred.
                  
                  
                    CONCLUSIONS:
                    A standardized spark-pattern cut-mode bailout workflow provides a reproducible framework for difficult left bundle branch area pacing lead deployment. Progression markers should be distinguished from procedural success, and follow-up surveillance remains essential. Larger studies with longer follow-up and dedicated lead-integrity testing are required before general adoption.
